name: Kai
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Clouse, Duane A. 1997. Towards a reconstruction and reclassification of the Lakes Plain languages of Irian Jaya. In Karl Franklin (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-85), 133-236. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A85.133 (open CC BY-SA edition, sealang.net).
catalog_locator: sec. 11 'Tone typology', p.152; Appendix 3 introduction, p.160; Kai word-list source note, p.163.
catalog_quote: [p.152, sec. 11 TONE TYPOLOGY] Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. This fact further distances Lakes Plain languages from the Trans New Guinea Phylum. All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. The remainder of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi (Kim 1995) and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.1). ... [p.160, Appendix 3] Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date. ... [p.163, word-list sources] Language: Kai / Elicitor(s): L. McAllister / Reliability: Obtained on survey. / Date: April 1986 / Transcription comments: The digraphs iy and uw represent a fricativised i and u. ... Most k's are backed. / Village: Kai

All the modem [scanned for modern] languages have at least high and low tone.' -- present verbatim (only difference: text reads 'modem', quote gives 'modern'; the compiler ellipsis skips one sentence about TNG). (2) p.28 = printed p.160, Appendix 3 intro: 'Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level only: Kai(y), one of the 20 Lakes Plain languages in Clouse's comparison (data = a 1986 survey word list), is covered by his statements that all Lakes Plain languages have at least a high/low tone contrast and that stress has not been found contrastive in any of them; no source says where stress falls in Kaiy. The nearest first-hand positional rule is for the sister language Doutai (McAllister & McAllister 1991 p.133: stress, realised as length, on the first syllable, non-phonemic), which is NOT a statement about Kaiy.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Clouse notes Sikaritai has been analysed as pitch accent and Iau has eight tones, but says nothing specific about Kai prosody.
new_statements.domain_note: Comparative survey based on 267-item word lists; the stress remark is a transcription note for the appendix word lists, not an analysis of Kaiy words or phrases.
new_statements.identity_note: Clouse 1997 calls the language 'Kai' (abbrev. Ka; village Kai); McAllister & McAllister 1991 and Voorhoeve 1975 call it 'Taori-Kei (Kaiy)'. All refer to kaiy1239 [tcq]. The only positional stress rule in the neighbourhood (first-syllable, non-phonemic) is for Doutai (dout1240), a different language in the same Glottolog subgroup 'Doutai-Kai-Waritai', in which Kaiy speakers are reported bilingual; it must not be filed under Kaiy.

sources.note: 'Kai' is one of the 20 languages in the study (250 speakers; word list L. McAllister, survey, April 1986, village Kai, p.163). Only family-level prosody: p.152 sec.11 all Lakes Plain languages have at least high and low tone; p.160 App.3 stress not marked in the lists because 'it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date'. Nothing on where stress falls in Kai.

sources.citation: McAllister, Lawrence and Kay McAllister. 1991. The process of phonological change in Doutai. In M. Hartzler & L. Wood (eds.), Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 9, 121-142. Jayapura: Cenderawasih University & SIL.
sources.note: About DOUTAI (dout1240), Kaiy's closest documented sister: p.133 sec.3.1 'Stress, often manifested by length, is found on the first syllable of the word. As such, it is not emic.' Editor's afterword pp.141-142 notes the first-syllable stress analysis was adopted 'across-the-board' and may yet be disproved. Kaiy appears only as 'Taori-Kei (Kaiy)' in Voorhoeve's family list (p.121), as having 'fricative' high vowels and no syllable closure in recent word lists (pp.138-139), and in note 1 p.140: Kaiy people 'are fluent in Doutai as well as their language'. No Kaiy stress statement.
